strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper identifies that mixed-type marginals (discrete point masses plus continuous density, e.g., zero-inflation, missingness) are poorly handled by unified diffusion objectives, and motivates the cascaded decomposition with empirical evidence (Figure 2a, 2b).

The cascaded flow matching framework is technically well-constructed: the guided conditional probability path with feature-specific learnable time schedules and data-dependent source distributions is a clean extension of flow matching (Equations 5-7), with correct derivations in Appendix A.1 and a valid reduction to standard FM as a special case.

Principled treatment of mixed-type features: discrete states (missing, inflated values) are decided by the low-resolution model and the high-resolution model masks those entries (Equation 2), which is a natural and arguably first-class way to handle such marginals within a diffusion pipeline.

Extensive and fairly designed evaluation: 12 diverse datasets (7 standard + 5 from TabZilla), 8 baselines including recent SOTA (TabDiff, CDTD), broad metric suite (C2ST detection, Shape, WD, JSD, Trend, MLE, alpha/beta precision-recall, DCR, MIA), 3 training seeds and 10 sampling seeds, with baselines aligned in architecture, parameter count, and training budget, including a sensible encoding-based mechanism to let baselines generate missing values.

Substantial ablation coverage: cascade factorization vs. latent augmentation, data-dependent coupling vs. independent, non-linear vs. linear paths, DT vs. GMM encoders, encoder-depth sweeps, missingness rates, and alternate low-resolution models (ARF), which convincingly isolate the contributions of the components (Table 2).

The transport cost result (Theorem 1, Appendix A.1.3) is correct and the honest treatment of privacy/diversity trade-offs (higher DCR share, slightly lower MIA) and of the residual fidelity/diversity tension strengthens credibility.
Strong reproducibility: full implementation details, algorithms for training and sampling, hyperparameters, training/sampling times, links to all baseline codebases, and stated code release.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution (Theorem 1) is incremental: the tightened transport bound follows fairly directly from constructing a source distribution with feature-wise means/variances closer to the target than a standardized independent coupling, and it relies on restrictive assumptions (DT encoder, standardized features, gamma_t identical across couplings) that limit its depth.

Exposure bias from teacher forcing is not analyzed: p_high is trained on ground-truth x_low = (x_cat, z) but at generation time is conditioned on samples from p_low; the paper does not quantify or experimentally probe the mismatch this induces (e.g., sensitivity to low-resolution model quality beyond the ARF ablation).

The headline 40% detection-score improvement rests on a single primary metric (C2ST with LightGBM); a high-fidelity model that better matches fine structure may also be more detectable by the very discretization artifacts it models, so corroborating evidence from other joint-distribution metrics or statistical two-sample tests would strengthen the claim. Standard deviations on the detection score are large (e.g., 0.423+/-0.370), making per-dataset conclusions uneven (Appendix A.8).

The novelty claim of 'first cascaded diffusion model for tabular data' and 'first diffusion model for mixed-type feature generation' should be stated more carefully: CoDi (Lee et al., 2023) explicitly targets mixed-type tabular synthesis (though not mixed marginals), and cascaded/hybrid discrete-continuous decomposition ideas exist in image generation (Tang et al., 2024; Sahoo et al., 2023); the contribution is a transfer and adaptation rather than an entirely new concept.

Part of the performance appears inherited from reusing CDTD as the low-resolution component; the framework's modularity is claimed as a strength, but the empirical gain attributable to the framework itself versus the CDTD low-res model could be more clearly disentangled.

The non-linear time schedules add complexity but yield only subtle gains (Table 2: non-linear paths barely change metrics), and the learned schedules in Appendix A.6.2 are close to linear on average, raising questions about whether this component justifies its complexity.

The comparison relies on strong baseline modifications (custom missingness masks for all baselines, architectural edits to TabDiff) that, while described in detail, could favor or disadvantage specific baselines in ways that are hard to verify without rerunning the benchmark.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: generating mixed-type numerical features (combining point masses, e.g., missingness and inflated values, with continuous densities) in tabular generative modeling, whereas prior work (TabDDPM, TabDiff, CDTD) cannot natively generate missing values in numerical features.

The cascaded framework is well-motivated: the empirical evidence in Figure 2a/23 that categorical features are substantially easier to generate than numerical ones provides a data-driven justification for the divide-and-conquer decomposition, and the low-resolution latent z is a clean mechanism for handling mixed-type marginals (Equation 2).

The experimental evaluation is unusually thorough: 12 diverse datasets, 8 baselines, a broad metric suite (detection score, Shape, WD, JSD, Trend, MLE, alpha/beta precision-recall, DCR, MIA), three training and ten sampling seeds, and per-dataset breakdowns in the appendix.

The ablation study (Table 2) carefully isolates each component (cascade alone, latents alone, FM switch, data-dependent coupling, non-linear paths, DT vs. GMM encoder), and additional ablations cover missingness rates, no-missing data, encoder complexity, and alternative low-resolution models.

Reproducibility appears solid: implementation details, architectures, hyperparameters, training/sampling times, licenses, and code availability are documented; the vector-field derivation and coupling proof are given in full in the appendix.
The model is efficient (Table 21/22: comparable or faster sampling than CDTD/TabDiff) and achieves gains with a comparable parameter budget.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is technically weak: it essentially shows that conditioning x0 on a coarse partition of x1 reduces the expected squared transport distance relative to an independent N(0, I) coupling, which follows almost directly from conditional expectation arguments. The 'tightens the transport cost bound' framing in the abstract oversells a straightforward observation, and the proof assumes gamma-dot is identical across couplings, which is not generally the case.

The headline 40% detection-score improvement deserves scrutiny: detection scores vary enormously across datasets (0.001 on news to 0.89 on adult; std ~0.37), and the improvement is concentrated in a few datasets. Moreover, the LightGBM-based C2ST is highly sensitive to missing-value patterns, which TabCascade generates natively while baselines use an encoding-based bolt-on — so part of the gain may reflect metric alignment with the proposed mechanism rather than uniformly superior joint-distribution fidelity.

Fidelity gains come at a diversity cost that is acknowledged but under-analyzed: DCR share moves further from the optimal 0.5 (0.891 vs. baselines), and high detection scores can partly indicate sharper, less diverse samples. A stronger treatment of this trade-off would be needed before the realism claims are fully convincing.

Training uses teacher forcing: p_high is trained on real xlow but at generation time conditions on sampled xlow. The resulting exposure-bias / distribution-shift gap is neither quantified nor ablated (e.g., training with sampled low-resolution outputs), leaving a potential train-test mismatch in the central mechanism.

Novelty is compositional: cascading (Ho et al.), data-dependent couplings (Albergo et al.), and learnable feature-specific time schedules (Sahoo et al.) are each existing techniques; the contribution is their adaptation to tabular data. The claim of being 'the first diffusion model to address mixed-type feature generation' should be stated more carefully given the imputation and zero-inflation literature. The ablation also shows non-linear paths contribute almost nothing (+0.002 detection score), and the GMM-encoder variant performs on par with vanilla CDTD (0.298 vs. 0.301), indicating strong sensitivity to the encoder choice.

Some experimental choices may disadvantage baselines: all diffusion baselines are capped at 30 minutes of training and use small 3M-parameter MLPs, and TabDiff's transformer components are stripped out. Whether reported gains persist under stronger baseline configurations is not established.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('compare the benefit of ... compared the average', 'leanable noise schedules', 'We advice'), a missing repository URL in the CDTD description, and 'first cascaded diffusion model for tabular data' claims in the introduction vs. 'flow matching' framing elsewhere could be tightened.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: mixed-type features (point masses at missing/inflated values) are not natively handled by existing tabular diffusion models, and the cascaded low-/high-resolution decomposition is a sensible, well-motivated design that naturally accommodates them via Equation (2).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 12 diverse datasets (including 5 additional TabZilla datasets), 8 baselines, multiple metrics (detection score, Shape, WD, JSD, Trend, MLE, precision/recall, DCR, MIA), 3 training and 10 sampling seeds, and extensive per-dataset results in the appendix.

Substantial empirical gains: the DT-encoder variant improves the detection score from 0.301 (best baseline CDTD) to 0.423 and roughly halves WD (num), with consistent per-dataset improvements (Tables 1 and 4).

Useful ablation program: Table 2 isolates the cascade, latents, flow matching switch, data-dependent coupling, and nonlinear paths; additional ablations cover missingness rate, complete data, encoder choice (DT vs. GMM vs. ARF), and encoder complexity (Figs. 24-25, Tables 17-20).

Reproducibility is strong: algorithmic training/generation pseudocode, detailed implementation and baseline alignment (same MLP budget of ~3M parameters, 30-minute training cap), encoder details, and a statement that all code and configuration files are released.
Writing and presentation are generally clear; the derivations in Appendix A.1 (guided conditional vector field, training target) are correct applications of Lipman et al.'s Theorem 3.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin and arguably trivial. Theorem 1 essentially shows that conditioning the source distribution on a DT partition reduces expected squared transport distance compared to a standard-normal source on standardized data - this follows from the optimality of conditional means. The proof also assumes the same time-derivative gamma_t regardless of the coupling, which is questionable since gamma_t is learnable and conditioned on x_low.

The ablation in Table 2 undercuts the narrative of the proposed components. Adding latents z to CDTD catastrophically degrades performance (detection 0.301 -> 0.104), and the recovery comes almost entirely from switching to a plain FM model with data-dependent coupling (0.104 -> 0.400 -> 0.421). The 'novel guided conditional probability path' (nonlinear paths) contributes almost nothing (0.421 -> 0.423), so the headline methodological novelty reduces mostly to a data-dependent coupling applied in a cascaded setting - both known ingredients (Albergo et al., 2024; Ho et al., 2022).

Fairness concerns in the baseline comparison: all baselines are retrofitted with a simple mean-imputation plus separate binary missingness-mask mechanism, which is a weak adaptation compared to TabCascade's native treatment. This inflates the gap on the missingness-focused evaluation, which is the paper's central claim.

No statistical significance analysis despite the paper's emphasis on averages: several results have very large standard deviations and high cross-dataset variance (e.g., detection 0.423+-0.370; airlines 0.589+-0.138 vs. CDTD 0.458+-0.021), and MLE/DCR/MIA results are mixed or only marginal relative to CDTD.

Teacher forcing (training p_high on real x_low but sampling from generated x_low) introduces an exposure-bias/distribution-shift concern that is acknowledged implicitly but never analyzed or ablated (e.g., no results training p_high on model-generated low-resolution samples).

The claim of 'first diffusion model to address mixed-type feature generation' needs qualification: the evaluation relies on simulated 10% MNAR missingness rather than datasets with genuine inflated/missing structure, and numerical features are quantile-transformed and standardized beforehand, which flattens exactly the marginal structure the cascade is claimed to capture - absolute WD gains (0.009 -> 0.004) are small in this scale.

Limitations are discussed only obliquely in the conclusion (future work on privacy, imputation, other modalities); there is no dedicated limitations section addressing e.g. encoder sensitivity, the CDTD dependency of the low-resolution component, or the two-model inference pipeline.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: mixed-type features (discrete point masses plus continuous density, e.g., missing/inflated/censored values) are genuinely not handled natively by existing tabular diffusion/flow models, and the paper clearly articulates why (Figure 2a, imbalanced losses in Figure 2b).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 12 diverse datasets (including the TabZilla suite), 7 strong baselines (CTGAN, TVAE, ARF, TabDDPM, TabSyn, TabDiff, CDTD), a broad metric suite (detection score, Shape, WD, JSD, Trend, MLE, alpha-Precision/beta-Recall, DCR, MIA), 3 training seeds and 10 sampling seeds, and extensive per-dataset results in the appendix.

Thorough ablations (Table 2) that isolate each component: cascade factorization, latent z, flow-matching high-resolution model, data-dependent coupling, non-linear paths, and DT vs. GMM encoders — convincingly showing each contributes.

Honest treatment of the fidelity–privacy tension: the paper reports MIA and DCR, explicitly warns that high fidelity harms privacy, and investigates overfitting via train-vs-test metrics (WD/JSD/Shape/Trend on test sets).

Good reproducibility: detailed implementation/hyperparameter alignment across baselines, training/sampling time tables, and code availability; missing-value simulation protocol (MAR+MCAR, MNAR) is documented.

The paper is generally well written, with clear exposition of the guided conditional probability path and derivations in the appendix; the framework is modular (any categorical generative model can serve as the low-resolution model, shown via ARF ablation).
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the paper is largely a careful composition of known ideas — cascaded diffusion (Ho et al., 2022; Saharia et al., 2022), data-dependent couplings (Albergo et al., 2024), learnable time schedules (Sahoo et al., 2024b), and CDTD as the low-resolution model — applied to tabular data. The main technical novelty is the guided conditional probability path, which is a relatively direct adaptation.

Theorem 1 is narrow and the proof is loose: it only compares the DT-based data-dependent coupling to an *independent* coupling with a standard Gaussian source, and the sufficient conditions (Eq. 15–16) use weak inequalities that would also be met trivially in many settings; the tightness claim ('provably lowers the transport cost bound') oversells a fairly elementary argument.

The entire motivation (mixed-type features) rests on *simulated* missingness (10% MNAR overlay). No evaluation on datasets with real, naturally occurring missing/inflated/censored values is provided, which limits the evidence that the method helps in the practical settings it targets.

The headline 51.9% detection-score improvement is an average driven largely by low-performing baselines; per-dataset gains over the strongest baseline (CDTD) vary, and the motivating Figure 2b weight-sweep is a single-dataset experiment.

Teacher-forcing training of p_high on real data while sampling from p_low at generation time introduces a potential train–sample mismatch (exposure bias) that is not analyzed; the paper notes it only as a 'reduced time penalty'.

The theoretical claim in the introduction that H(x_num|z) < H(x_num|x_cat) justifying the latent z is asserted rather than substantiated, and the cascade could in principle hurt cross-type dependency modeling (addressed only empirically via Trend (mixed)).
Some baseline results are missing (TabDDPM NaNs on airlines, diabetes, news; TabDiff sampling time outlier), slightly weakening the completeness of comparisons.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and under-served problem: mixed-type features (discrete point masses combined with continuous densities, e.g., zero-inflation, censoring, informative missingness) are not explicitly modeled by prior tabular diffusion models, and the motivation (Figure 2a/b) is empirically grounded.

The cascaded design is well-motivated: the low-resolution latent z gives the high-resolution flow matching model a data-dependent coupling and learnable, xlow-conditioned time schedules, and the guided conditional probability path and vector field are derived correctly from Lipman et al.'s framework (Appendix A.1.1/A.1.2).

The evaluation is unusually thorough: 12 diverse datasets, 8 baselines including the strongest recent ones (TabDiff, CDTD), 3 training seeds × 10 sampling seeds, a broad metric suite (C2ST detection, Shape, WD, JSD, Trend, MLE, α-Precision/β-Recall, DCR, MIA), and fair adaptation of baselines that cannot natively generate missings.

The ablation study (Table 2) cleanly disentangles the contributions: cascaded factorization alone improves CDTD, the latent z without the coupling/path changes hurts, and the full model recovers large gains; this transparently identifies which components matter, including that non-linear paths contribute only marginally.

Potential overfitting is probed directly (train vs. test metrics, MIA), the fidelity–privacy trade-off is honestly discussed, and implementation details (algorithms, hyperparameters, training times) are extensive, supporting reproducibility; code is stated to be available.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin and loosely argued. Theorem 1 is a straightforward variance-decomposition argument, its proof relies on sufficient conditions (e.g., the claim that σ²_z(i) ≤ 1 'directly follows' from interval containment within the support of a standardized variable is not rigorous, and the assumption that γ̇_t is identical across couplings is convenient), and it holds only for the DT encoder, not the GMM variant also proposed.

Novelty is incremental: cascaded generation (Ho et al., 2022), data-dependent couplings (Albergo et al., 2024), and feature-specific learnable schedules (CDTD, TabDiff) are all established; the paper's main new element is the univariate discretization of numerical features into bins/leaves as a conditioning latent, which is conceptually close to classical quantization/discretization rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Missingness is entirely synthetic (10% MNAR injected by the authors) and inflated-value prevalence in the benchmarks is not quantified; the paper never evaluates on a dataset with naturally occurring missings or inflation, so the central claim of faithful mixed-type generation is validated only on the authors' own simulation.

There is a train/sampling mismatch: p_high is trained with teacher forcing on true xlow but sampled with p_low-generated xlow; no analysis (e.g., sensitivity to p_low quality is only touched via the ARF ablation) of how error in p_low propagates, and the ARF ablation shows a large detection-score drop (0.782 → 0.494), suggesting sensitivity to this gap.

The '51.9% improvement in detection score' headline rests on a single C2ST metric whose detector could be sensitive to artifacts (e.g., discrete-state placement, rounding post-processing); per-dataset results (Table 4) show notable variance (e.g., 0.595±0.143 on airlines, only 0.202 on news), and gains on some metrics (JSD (cat), MIA, DCR) favor other baselines.

The claim of being 'the first diffusion model to address mixed-type feature generation' is overstated: prior work (e.g., CoDi, VAEM) targets mixed-type tabular data, and the distinction to per-feature mixed marginals is not crisply delineated until deep in Section 3.

Comparability concerns: diffusion baselines are capped at 30 minutes training and all methods are re-implemented with a common MLP architecture, which may disadvantage methods relying on their native designs (TabDiff's transformer parts are removed); no statistical significance tests are reported for headline comparisons.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and previously unserved gap: existing tabular diffusion models cannot generate informative missing/inflated values in numerical features, and mixed-type marginals lack dedicated treatment. TabCascade's low-resolution discrete states give a natural mechanism for this, and the paper demonstrates the capability directly.

The motivation is supported by empirical evidence (Figure 2: categorical features are easier to generate than numerical ones; loss-weight tuning of CDTD improves realism), which makes the divide-and-conquer design principled rather than ad hoc.

The guided conditional probability path with data-dependent couplings and learnable, feature-specific time schedules is cleanly derived; the CFM loss (Eq. 6) reduces to the standard linear-path loss in the degenerate setting, showing the formulation is a strict generalization.

Comprehensive evaluation: 12 datasets (7 from prior work + 5 from TabZilla), strong baselines including very recent TabDiff and CDTD, three training and ten sampling seeds, a broad metric suite (detection score, Shape/WD/JSD, Trend, MLE, alpha-Precision/beta-Recall, DCR, MIA), and extensive ablations (cascade, latents, coupling, schedules, encoder choice, encoder depth, missingness rate, alternative low-resolution model, training without missings).

The ablation table is informative and honest: it shows the cascade alone helps, that adding latents z to CDTD *hurts* (an interesting negative result the authors explain via learnable noise schedules), and that the combination of coupling + flow matching drives most of the gain.

Reproducibility is strong: code and configuration files, detailed algorithms for training and generation, aligned architectures/parameter budgets across baselines (~3M parameters, 30-minute training cap), and full per-dataset result tables in the appendix.

The paper treats evaluation caveats seriously: it separates train- vs test-set metrics to check overfitting, reports MIA and discusses the fidelity-privacy trade-off, and explicitly states that DCR should be read as a diversity metric (Yao et al., 2025).
weaknesses: Memorization signals warrant scrutiny: detection scores reach ~1.0 on credit_g and phoneme, and DCR share reaches 1.000/0.990 on those datasets, meaning synthetic samples are essentially maximally close to training records. The train-vs-test gap analysis and still-high MIA scores mitigate but do not fully resolve this concern, and it suggests the headline 51.9% detection-score gain may partly reflect near-memorization on small datasets rather than purely better distribution learning.

The theory (Theorem 1) is modest: the proof reduces to showing the per-feature in-cluster MSE is at most the marginal variance under standardized data, and relies on assumptions (standardized features, DT interval partitions, shared gamma_t) that limit generality. It supports the design but is not a deep result.

Attribution of gains between the proposed components is somewhat muddled by the fact that p_low is CDTD itself; the largest jump comes from switching the high-resolution model to flow matching with data-dependent coupling (0.518 -> 0.786), while 'cascade' and 'non-linear paths' contribute comparatively little (0.694 and 0.787 vs 0.786). The framing as a contribution of the cascaded pipeline somewhat overstates the role of cascading per se.

The baseline augmentation for missing-value generation (mean-imputed values plus a separate categorical missingness mask) is a reasonable but simple workaround; baselines were not designed for this setting, so the marginal comparison on the mixed-type task is somewhat favorable to the proposed method by construction.

Evaluation relies heavily on the detection score as the primary metric; while multiple auxiliary metrics corroborate the gains, detection-score differences can be sensitive to the classifier capacity and post-processing (the paper itself notes precision alignment is 'crucial').

Minor presentation issues: incomplete code URL in the abstract, occasional typos ('leanable', 'We advice'), and the main text leans on the appendix for several key results (encoder details, ablations), which slightly impairs readability of the core narrative.
